modelAnswer: Neurons in crude touch pathway from body: (1st) Dorsal root ganglion cell - peripheral process receives touch, central process enters spinal cord and ascends/descends 1-2 segments in Lissauer's tract; (2nd) Neuron in nucleus proprius of posterior horn (laminae III, IV) - axon decussates in anterior white commissure and ascends in ventral spinothalamic tract; (3rd) Neuron in VPL nucleus of thalamus - axon projects to postcentral gyrus via posterior limb of internal capsule.

Neurons in conscious proprioception and fine touch pathway: (1st) Dorsal root ganglion cell - peripheral receptor receives stimulus, central process ascends ipsilaterally in dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis/cuneatus); (2nd) Neuron in gracile/cuneate nuclei of medulla - axon decussates as internal arcuate fibers and ascends as medial lemniscus to VPL of thalamus; (3rd) Neuron in VPL of thalamus - axon passes through posterior limb of internal capsule to postcentral gyrus.

Tracts for proprioception: (A) CONSCIOUS proprioception: Gracile tract (lower body) and Cuneate tract (upper body). (B) UNCONSCIOUS proprioception: (1) Posterior spinocerebellar tract (from Clarke's nucleus, lower body); (2) Anterior spinocerebellar tract (lower body); (3) Cuneocerebellar tract (from accessory cuneate nucleus, upper body).

Unconscious proprioception to cerebellum: (1) From lower body: Muscle spindles/Golgi tendon organs → dorsal root ganglion (1st) → Clarke's nucleus (2nd) → posterior spinocerebellar tract (or anterior) → inferior cerebellar peduncle → cerebellum. (2) From upper body: Same → accessory cuneate nucleus (2nd) → cuneocerebellar tract → inferior cerebellar peduncle → cerebellum.

Pain pathway from face and body: BODY: (1st) DRG → Lissauer's tract → posterior horn; (2nd) Substantia gelatinosa → decussates → lateral spinothalamic tract; (3rd) VPL thalamus → postcentral gyrus. FACE: (1st) Trigeminal ganglion → spinal nucleus CN V; (2nd) Decussates → trigeminal lemniscus; (3rd) VPM thalamus → postcentral gyrus. Both pathways converge at thalamus and cortex but use different nuclei.

Touch sensations of the face are carried by: (1) Discriminative (fine) touch: Principal (main) sensory nucleus of CN V → ventral trigeminothalamic tract → VPM of thalamus → postcentral gyrus. (2) Crude touch: Spinal nucleus of CN V → ventral trigeminothalamic tract → VPM of thalamus. Both pathways use the trigeminal nerve and its sensory nuclei.

Pyramidal tract lamination: (A) CEREBRAL CORTEX: Arises from motor areas 4, 6, and adjacent areas; fibers descend through corona radiata. (B) INTERNAL CAPSULE: Passes through posterior limb (somatotopic: face most anterior, leg most posterior). (C) BRAIN STEM: Passes through basis pedunculi of midbrain (medial 3/5), basis pontis (scattered bundles), medullary pyramids. (D) MEDULLA: In pyramidal decussation, fibers destined for arm decussate first (become lateral CST), those for leg remain ipsilateral then decussate lower. (E) SPINAL CORD: Lateral CST has cervical fibers most medial, sacral most lateral.

Termination of pyramidal tract: The lateral corticospinal tract terminates on alpha motor neurons (final common pathway) and gamma motor neurons in the anterior horn of all spinal segments. The anterior corticospinal tract (uncrossed) terminates similarly but only in upper segments. Corticobulbar fibers terminate on cranial nerve motor nuclei in the brainstem.

Corticobulbar (corticomotor) tract: (ORIGIN) Precentral and postcentral gyri, frontal eye fields; (COURSE) Descends through posterior limb of internal capsule, basis pedunculi of midbrain, basis pontis, medullary pyramids; (TERMINATION) On motor nuclei of cranial nerves (CN III, IV, V, VI, VII, IX, X, XI, XII); (CONNECTIONS) Most CN nuclei receive BILATERAL input (except lower facial nucleus - mainly contralateral, and trochlear nucleus).

Tectospinal tract: (ORIGIN) Superior colliculus of midbrain; (COURSE) Decussates immediately below its origin, descends in spinal cord (most fibers terminate in upper cervical segments); (FUNCTION) Reflex turning of head and neck in response to visual and auditory stimuli (spino-visual and spino-auditory reflexes); (CLINICAL) Lesion causes inability to turn head toward stimuli.

Rubrospinal tract: (ORIGIN) Red nucleus (magnocellular part) of midbrain; (COURSE) Decussates immediately, descends through brain stem, enters lateral white column of spinal cord; (FUNCTION) Facilitates flexor muscle tone, inhibits extensor tone; (RELATION) Takes over function of corticospinal tract after lesion; (CLINICAL) Lesion causes decerebrate rigidity.

Blood supply of cervical spinal cord: (1) VERTEBRAL ARTERIES → anterior spinal artery (formed at medulla) and two posterior spinal arteries; (2) ANTERIOR SPINAL ARTERY supplies anterior 2/3 of cord (anterior horn, lateral horn, anterior and lateral white columns); (3) POSTERIOR SPINAL ARTERIES supply posterior 1/3 (posterior horn, posterior columns); (4) RADICULAR ARTERIES from vertebral, ascending cervical, and deep cervical arteries reinforce the longitudinal arteries.

Anterior spinal artery: (ORIGIN) Formed by union of two anterior spinal branches of vertebral arteries at the medulla; (COURSE) Descends in anterior median fissure; (PARTS SUPPLIED) (1) Anterior 2/3 of spinal cord; (2) Anterior horn (motor); (3) Lateral horn (sympathetic); (4) Anterior and lateral white columns; (5) Gray commissure (with crossing fibers).

Posterior spinal arteries: (ORIGIN) Usually from posterior inferior cerebellar arteries (PICA) or vertebral arteries; (COURSE) Descends as two vessels near dorsal roots; (PARTS SUPPLIED) (1) Posterior 1/3 of spinal cord; (2) Posterior horn; (3) Posterior columns; (4) Posterior white columns. Note: Posterior spinal arteries are often discontinuous and reinforced by radicular arteries.

Arteries giving radicular arteries: (1) VERTEBRAL ARTERIES; (2) ASCENDING CERVICAL ARTERIES (branch of inferior thyroid); (3) DEEP CERVICAL ARTERIES (branch of costocervical trunk); (4) INTERCOSTAL ARTERIES (for thoracic segments); (5) LUMBAR ARTERIES (for lumbar segments); (6) LATERAL SACRAL ARTERIES (for sacral segments).

UMN vs LMN lesion differences: (UMN) Spastic paralysis, hypertonia, hyperreflexia, clonus, positive Babinski, no muscle atrophy (or minimal); (LMN) Flaccid paralysis, hypotonia, hyporeflexia/areflexia, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, no Babinski. UMN lesion affects descending corticospinal pathways; LMN affects peripheral motor neurons or their cell bodies.

Two main tracts in hemisection: (1) LATERAL CORTICOSPINAL TRACT - controls voluntary movement; lesion causes ipsilateral UMN paralysis below level of lesion; (2) SPINOTHALAMIC TRACTS - carry pain and temperature; lesion causes contralateral loss of pain/temperature (after decussation) below lesion. Other tracts affected: posterior columns (ipsilateral loss of proprioception/fine touch).

Complete transection of spinal cord: (IMMEDIATE) Spinal shock - flaccid paralysis, loss of all sensations, absent reflexes below lesion; (AFTER WEEKS) Spastic paralysis, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski; (SENSORY) Loss of pain, temperature, touch, proprioception below lesion; (AUTONOMIC) Loss of bladder/bowel control, sexual dysfunction; (LEVEL) All functions lost at and below the lesion.

Brown-Sequard syndrome (hemisection): (1) IPSILATERAL to lesion: UMN paralysis below; loss of conscious proprioception and fine touch (dorsal columns); (2) CONTRALATERAL to lesion: Loss of pain and temperature starting 1-2 segments below (spinothalamic); (3) At lesion level: LMN signs at exact segment, and loss of all sensations at that level.

Anterior spinal artery occlusion: (AREA AFFECTED) Anterior 2/3 of spinal cord; (CLINICAL) Bilateral loss of motor function (anterior horn) → flaccid then spastic paralysis; bilateral loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic tracts); PRESERVED: dorsal column functions (proprioception, vibration, fine touch) bilaterally.

Sensory loss in syringomyelia: (1) BILATERAL cape-like loss of pain and temperature (due to damage to crossing spinothalamic fibers in anterior white commissure); (2) Touch sensation partially preserved (dorsal columns intact); (3) Proprioception preserved; (4) Sensory loss begins in upper limbs and may extend to trunk and lower limbs; (5) 'Dissociated sensory loss' - loss of pain/temperature with preserved touch.
